source.title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study removes examples selected by a subsampled memorization estimate and compares the resulting test accuracy with removal of the same number of random examples. It tests the effect of removing memorized examples on generalization using a different estimator and intervention than a direct memorization-capacity/generalization comparison.
record.gate_note: The study tests the utility of removing examples selected by its memorization estimator and reports comparisons with random removal. Its discussion of random-label fitting and generalization cites Zhang et al. and Arpit et al.; those cited findings are not rows. It does not test the claim versions about memorization capacity coexisting with natural-label generalization, width, architecture comparisons, optimizer, batch size, dropout, or sharpness.
record.test_reason: This is the original source for V8. Its own experiments compare test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples with accuracy after removing equally many random examples. The subsampled inclusion-based memorization estimator is the method underlying V8, not a different replication recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that memorizing atypical training examples improves accuracy on visually similar test examples, supporting the long-tail explanation; the benefit depends on data variability and sample availability. They also conclude that most measured memorization occurs in learned representations before the final layer.
record.recipe_differences: Uses subsampled estimates of self-memorization and influence, then removes selected examples and compares accuracy with random removal; it does not test the original claim's direct random-label fitting/generalization recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect on accuracy depends on dataset variability and number of examples. Architecture changes affect estimate consistency and correlate with model accuracy; the last-layer-only linear-model estimator detects far fewer memorized examples than full-network training.

fits_no_version.finding: With fixed representations learned from the full CIFAR-100 dataset, final-layer models identify only 38 examples above the memorization threshold, versus 18,099 when retraining the full network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most measured label memorization is already encoded in learned representations before the final classifier.

record.problems: The method requires thousands of model trainings. Threshold selection can introduce selection bias, especially for influence estimates near the threshold. The authors state their architectures and training algorithms are not state-of-the-art. Figure 2's threshold-specific accuracy values are not given in text.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted for the tested version. The linear-model versus full-ResNet memorization counts and test accuracies in section 3.6 do not directly measure removal effects or a listed version; the representation finding is noted under fits_no_version but no row is included because the mapped version set does not cover it.

untested.parts: No own experiment compares random-label fitting with natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or test of generalization beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or intervention on local connectivity.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of generalization-gap rankings.

record.verdict_notes: Verdicts for V8 are suppressed because this study is its original source. The high-influence removal results belong with V8 as evidence about the removal effect, rather than under fits_no_version. Missing numerical precision in a figure does not itself establish a scope limitation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels; the relevant observations are cited prior work.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks trained from scratch; architecture comparisons concern consistency of memorization and influence estimates.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.

The study tests removal of examples selected by memorization estimates and comparison to random removal on MNIST, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. It does not test the exact influence-based inclusion criterion and ResNet-50 scope stated in V8 as a single claim; the study uses memorization estimates and reports architecture-specific CIFAR-100 analyses.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on subsets of the training dataset; 70% subsets for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Removed training examples whose estimated memorization was at or above a threshold and retrained; threshold varied.
rows.measure: Test accuracy after removing examples with memorization value estimates above a given threshold.
rows.baseline: Accuracy after removing the same number of randomly chosen examples; figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Shaded area represents one standard deviation on 5 trials.
rows.note: The text describes a significant effect of removal and higher marginal utility for memorized examples overall, but does not state ImageNet-specific values or direction relative to random removal in words.
rows.check: Section 1.1 supplies a numerical comparison: about 32% of ImageNet examples have memorization estimates ≥0.3; removing them costs approximately 3.4 percentage points of accuracy, versus approximately 2.6 points for equally many random examples. Replace 'figure only' accordingly. The 70% subsets are used to estimate memorization, not a fixed training fraction for the removal experiment.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on the full CIFAR-100 training set and with selected examples removed
rows.operation_detail: Removed the unique training examples in detected high-influence pairs, then retrained.

conditions.value: unique training examples in high-influence pairs

rows.baseline: 76.06 ± 0.28% accuracy on the full training set.
rows.uncertainty: Reported as ± values over 100 random runs.
rows.note: Removal criterion is membership in high-influence pairs, which also requires estimated memorization ≥ 0.25 and influence ≥ 0.15.
rows.check: The numerical removal result is correct. This tests the accuracy-loss component using a narrower selection requiring both memorization ≥0.25 and influence ≥0.15; it does not independently establish the comparison with random removal.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V8's comparison with equal-sized random removal. The full-test accuracy loss is observed, but this experiment compares full-data training with removal of high-influence training examples and supplies no random-removal control.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, lines 595–607; selection criteria in section 2.
source_check.problem: The observed accuracy loss alone cannot establish V8's comparative random-removal effect.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on the full CIFAR-100 training set and with selected examples removed
rows.operation_detail: Removed the unique training examples in detected high-influence pairs, then evaluated on the highly influenced test examples.
rows.measure: Accuracy on highly influenced test examples.
rows.uncertainty: Reported as ± values over 100 random runs.
rows.note: The authors state this difference contributes 2.38 ± 0.17% to the total difference in accuracy.
rows.check: The numerical result is correct, but concerns the selected highly influenced test subset. It explains the overall removal effect rather than independently testing the equal-count random-removal comparison.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V8's comparison with equal-sized random removal. Accuracy on the selected highly influenced test subset falls from 72.14 ± 1.32% to 45.38 ± 1.45%, using full-data training as baseline.
source_check.problem: This selected-subset comparison explains the accuracy loss but does not measure the random-controlled removal effect.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained after randomly selected examples were removed
rows.operation_detail: Removed a random set of training examples matching the count of examples removed by the memorization-threshold procedure.
rows.measure: Test accuracy after removing random training examples.
rows.baseline: Figure 2 compares with removal of examples selected by memorization value estimate; figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Shaded area represents one standard deviation on 100 (CIFAR-100, MNIST) and 5 (ImageNet) trials.
rows.note: The comparison is reported as a baseline in the figure; no dataset-specific numerical values are stated in text.
rows.check: This duplicates the comparator already included in R1–R3 and should be incorporated into those rows rather than treated as an independent effect. It also combines different datasets and architectures: MNIST uses simplified Inception.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR-100 subsets of 70% of the training set
rows.operation_detail: Compared full-dataset training with removal of all unique training examples in high-influence pairs.
rows.measure: Difference in test accuracy attributable to removal on highly influenced test examples.
rows.value: 2.38 ± 0.17% contribution to total difference in accuracy.
rows.note: Authors say this contribution is within one standard deviation of the entire accuracy difference.
rows.check: This is a derived decomposition of R4–R5, not an independent removal experiment. The 2.38 ±0.17 figure is a percentage-point contribution to the full-test accuracy difference. The experiment retrains on the full dataset and its complement after selected removal, not fixed 70% subsets.
